svg.title: Target group health and target lifecycle
svg.text: How a target group decides who gets traffic
The life of one Fargate task inside a target group, and what the ALB does when a group has nobody to serve.
Task starts
ECS launches it
initial
registered, being checked
no traffic
healthy
passing health checks
gets traffic
unhealthy
failing health checks
no new traffic
draining
deregistering
in-flight only
removed
gone from the group
What each step means
ECS registers the new task’s IP : port in the target group (you never add it by hand).
A newly registered target needs to pass just one health check → the ALB starts routing to it. (A target recovering from unhealthy needs N passes in a row — the healthy threshold.)
It fails N checks in a row (unhealthy threshold) → the ALB stops sending it new requests.
The task is stopping: a new deployment, scale-in, or ECS replacing an unhealthy task.
In-flight requests finish or the deregistration delay (300 s by default) runs out; open WebSockets are then closed.
ECS sees the task is unhealthy by the load balancer, stops it and launches a replacement.
Two different health checks in your stack
Target-group health check
Sent by the ALB over the network to task-IP:port/healthz.
Decides whether that task receives traffic.
Container health check (task definition)
Runs inside the container: wget http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz.
Tells ECS whether the container process is alive.
Neither uses /acp — it only accepts WebSocket upgrades,
so a plain GET would fail and mark every agent task unhealthy.
When a target group has nobody to serve
0 registered targets → the ALB returns HTTP 503
The mcp-down drill: MCP service scaled to 0, so /mcp returns 503
and the agent answers with a “can’t reach the tools” sentence.
All targets unhealthy → the ALB “fails open”
It routes to all of them anyway: a maybe beats a certain 503.
Other target groups are unaffected
While /mcp is down, the WebUI (default) and /acp keep working —
each group’s health is independent.
